claims.text: A multiscale method that separately models lattice and electronic heat transport will predict temperature-dependent thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than previous methods.
Separate ab initio electron-transport calculations and anharmonic phonon-scattering calculations will predict measured thermal conductivity within approximately 20% over 50–1200 K.
The lattice and electronic contributions to heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable below 200 K.
HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen has a total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m) between 300 and 1200 K.
A sample containing less than 0.1 wt.% oxygen represents the alloy's relatively pure transport behavior.
The proposed lattice calculation includes explicit phonon–phonon and defect-scattering processes.
The proposed electronic thermal-transport calculation uses DFT-derived properties and perturbative methods such as the Kubo–Greenwood formalism.
Below 200 K is the regime in which experiments indicate comparable electronic and phonon contributions.
Controlled atmosphere and bulk-like specimen geometry minimize extrinsic scattering effects.
The lattice heat-transport channel is mediated by phonon–phonon interactions and is modulated by point defects and minor oxygen impurities.
The electronic heat-transport channel is governed by electron–phonon coupling determined from electronic band structures.
Explicit anharmonic lattice dynamics captures the temperature dependence of phonon lifetimes and scattering.
Using a distinct physical model for each transport contribution reduces errors caused by conflating lattice and electronic heat transport.
The method will predict total thermal conductivity within approximately 20% of measurements over the specified temperature range.
For samples containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, the method will predict total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Previous predictive approaches often have errors exceeding 40% relative to experimental measurements.
Previous predictive approaches conflated lattice and electronic contributions.
Previous predictive approaches did not capture the low-temperature crossover between lattice and electronic contributions.
The method may become less accurate for substantially more impure or nanocrystalline HfNbTaTiZr because additional scattering mechanisms can dominate.
Phonon-scattering predictions are sensitive to small changes in defect content, while electron–phonon interactions are difficult to quantify at extreme temperatures.
